shortDescription: Copper is the conducting metal of modern war. Washington has put copper on its critical-minerals list. Beijing is stockpiling it. But India, which imports more than 90% of its Copper Concentrate, has just diluted its stake in the country’s only copper miner — for a measly Rs 3,000 crore.Story Behin…

children: Copper is the conducting metal of modern war. Washington has put copper on its critical-minerals list. Beijing is stockpiling it. But India, which imports more than 90% of its Copper Concentrate, has just diluted its stake in the country’s only copper miner — for a measly Rs 3,000 crore.
Story Behind Government of India's Hindustan Copper Stake Sale.
Are some bureaucrats in New Delhi selling the country's most strategic asset cheap?
Washington is treating copper as a national-security asset.
Beijing is stockpiling it and tightening the gates around its mines. In contrast, New Delhi sold 6 percent of India's only company that can legally mine copper. All for roughly Rs 3,000 crore.
That is the strange arithmetic behind India’s latest disinvestment decision of Hindustan Copper.

In a surprising decision, the Government of India sold part of a strategic asset that cannot be replicated or substituted domestically, and sits at the centre of the Global Race for a metal now critical to defence, electricity, artificial intelligence, electric vehicles and the next generation of industrial infrastructure.

No, the government did not sell a failing company, a loss-making factory or an unwanted piece of land. It sold part of India’s only domestic source of a metal that has suddenly become strategic to the world’s two largest powers. And it sold it at a steep discount.
On August 26, the government completed the sale of 6 percent of Hindustan Copper at a floor price of Rs 514 a share, cutting its holding to about 60.14 per cent from  from 66.14 per cent.

The offer was roughly 10 percent below the prevailing market price and 32 per cent below the year’s high. The amount raised was Rs 3,000 crore - a measly figure in India's large balance sheet. Given the shape of geopolitics globally, the asset being diluted is rather harder to put a number on.
And the discounter is much steeper than it appears.
Hindustan Copper: India’s Prized Asset
Hindustan Copper is not one copper producer among many. It is the only Indian company with operating copper mining leases — all of them.

The country has smelters. It has refiners. It has ambitious plans to expand copper manufacturing, and two of its largest industrial houses have built plants for it. What it does not have is another company pulling copper ore out of Indian soil at scale.
Not Adani. Not Hindalco. Not Vedanta. Not any foreign major.
India can build another refinery, another smelter or send its companies abroad to buy mines.
But it cannot manufacture a second Malanjkhand.

A copper mine is not a factory that can be replicated by cutting a cheque. Geological deposits take millions of years to form, decades to find and prove, and years more to permit and develop. Globally, the lead time from discovery to first production now runs to fifteen years or longer.
Hindustan Copper’s advantage is not merely the metal it sells today. It is its control over the entire domestic geological pipeline.
That is the thing a 6 per cent slice was carved out of.
The Size of What Was Sold
As of April 1, 2025, Hindustan Copper reported reserves and resources of 767.37 million tonnes of ore at an average grade of 0.94 per cent under the United Nations Framework Classification.

That implies roughly 7.2 million tonnes of contained copper. At the record London Metal Exchange price struck on September 7, the gross in-situ value of that contained metal is on the order of Rs 8.9 lakh crore. Yes, you read it right. India diluted its stake in the company at below  Rs 50,000 crores.
Ore in the ground is not cash in the bank.

It has to be mined, milled, processed and moved; recovery rates, operating costs, royalties, capital expenditure and the sheer passage of time all take their cut. No serious valuation treats every tonne underground as money available today, and no mining company on earth trades at the worth of the metal beneath it. But the fact that the U.S. and China are stockpiling copper makes this India's most strategic asset.
The comparison exposes something more important than a valuation quibble.
Hindustan Copper’s entire stock-market value is around Rs 48,800 crore.

India’s only domestic copper miner is being valued by the market at roughly One Rupee for every Eighteen Rupees of gross metal it controls underground — before anyone assigns a price to scarcity, to strategic access, to future discoveries, or to the extraordinary fact that there is no domestic substitute for its mining position.
Apply that to the slice that changed hands.
The 6 per cent sold carries with it roughly 432,000 tonnes of contained copper in the reported resource base — a gross in-situ metal value of about Rs 53,000 crore at the September 7 price.
Against that, the government raised approximately Rs 3,000 crore.
Rs 3,000 crore is a large sum to an individual investor.

On the balance sheet of the Government of India, it is a rounding error. Set against a strategic resource whose gross metal value runs into several lakh crore, it is the reason this sale deserves scrutiny.
And the Asset is Not Static
The government was not selling down a depleting oil well with a known end date.
Hindustan Copper’s reported resource base stood at 631.85 million tonnes of ore in 2021-22.

By April 2025 it had reached 767.37 million tonnes. Since 2018, the company says it has added 198.61 million tonnes — roughly 28 million tonnes a year — without acquiring another copper company or buying another mine. It found it by drilling ground it already owned.
Even the flagship deposit has not been exhausted on paper.

A public hearing document filed with the Madhya Pradesh Pollution Control Board describes Malanjkhand as 2,600 metres long, 142 metres wide and 900 metres deep, and records it as “open for exploration at depth across and along strike.” Bishimetal Exploration Company of Tokyo, engaged to study the deposit, explored it to 600 metres.
Published geological literature traces mineralisation to approximately one kilometre.
In mining language, an ore body that is open at depth has not been closed off. Its floor has never been established.
The National picture is Starker Still

The Geological Survey of India has mapped an Obvious Geological Potential area of roughly half a million square kilometres, of which less than 10 per cent has been explored in any detail and under 2 per cent has ever been mined, according to analysis published by Brookings India.
India holds roughly 2 percent of global copper resources.

Domestic demand is forecast to reach 3 to 3.3 million tonnes by 2030 and up to 9.8 million tonnes by 2047. Import dependence on concentrate, already above 90 per cent, is projected to approach 97 per cent. Every tonne of that shortfall has to be bought abroad, in a market where supply is contracting.
India was therefore diluting a percentage of an asset whose measured size rises every year and whose ultimate extent nobody has established, in a country that has barely looked for more.
It was not a Distressed Asset.
It was a Rising One.
The sale was not forced by weakness.

Hindustan Copper had just delivered its best year on record. Revenue rose 49 per cent to Rs 3,077.92 crore in 2025-26. Net profit almost doubled to Rs 920.67 crore. The EBITDA margin reached 48.7 per cent.

The June 2026 quarter, the last reported before the sale, was stronger still: revenue up 81 per cent to Rs 936.50 crore, net profit up 162 per cent to Rs 352.37 crore, EBITDA up 139 per cent at a 54 per cent margin.
The company is nearly debt-free.
It is deploying Rs 7,188.6 crore of its own capital to triple mining capacity from 4.0 to 12.2 million tonnes of ore a year.
There was no fire sale because the company was burning cash. There was a sale because the government wanted cash. It did not need the money. The government did.
While Washington and Beijing were securing copper, India is monetising it Cheaply.
On November 7, 2025, the United States Geological Survey published the final 2025 List of Critical Minerals in the Federal Register.
Copper was added for the first time — one of ten new entries on a list of 60.

The designation is not symbolic. Inclusion determines which commodities fall inside Section 232 investigations, the statute under which the United States imposes tariffs on national-security grounds. Washington has already used it on semi-finished copper products.
Beijing has gone further.

China’s state-backed metals industry association called in February for an expansion of the country’s strategic copper stockpiles, urging coordination with state-owned producers to build commercial inventories. Estimates place China’s strategic reserves of critical minerals including copper at between 35 and 133 per cent of annual domestic demand.
In May, China announced new mining controls, effective June 15.

They impose security reviews on foreign investment in the Chinese mining sector and require strategic mineral reserves to be stored at source for a minimum of five years. China already restricts exports of rare earths, gallium, germanium and graphite.
One country is securing supply.
Another is treating it as a weapon. India sold part of its only domestic mining platform.
This is where India’s Rs 3,000 crore becomes difficult to ignore. The United States is worried enough about copper to put it inside its national-security machinery.

China is worried enough to stockpile it and restrict access to its mines. India owns one of the world’s scarcest forms of copper exposure — a domestic mining monopoly in a country overwhelmingly dependent on imports — and chose this moment to sell some of it.
Why Copper Became a Weapon
The reclassification is being driven by more than electric vehicles and solar panels.

Copper is the conducting metal of modern war: ammunition and shell casings, radar and avionics wiring, naval propulsion and shipboard systems, drones, guided munitions, battlefield communications. Defence-related copper demand is projected to triple by 2040.
It is also the binding physical constraint on the artificial intelligence build-out, where power distribution inside data centres consumes copper at multiples of conventional infrastructure.
And the economics of the industry have already turned in favour of whoever owns the ore rather than whoever processes it.

Antofagasta of Chile settled its 2026 annual treatment and refining charge with a Chinese smelter at zero dollars a tonne in December 2025, the lowest annual benchmark on record. Spot charges have fallen as low as minus $126.80 a tonne — smelters now paying miners for the right to process their ore.
That leaves India’s smelter-led strategy structurally exposed.
Adani’s Kutch Copper, the country’s largest single-location smelter, and Hindalco’s Birla Copper are formidable industrial assets. Neither owns an Indian mine. Both import nearly all their feed.

Hindustan Copper, meanwhile, is conducting due diligence with NTPC Mining and Coal India on the acquisition of four copper blocks from Chile’s state-owned Codelco, and reportedly intends to sell the resulting concentrate to Hindalco and Adani.
The state miner was being diluted at precisely the moment it was positioning itself as the country’s strategic supplier.
The Rs 3,000-crore Sale
Announced: August 24, 2026, via exchange filing. Sold August 25 (non-retail) and August 26 (retail).
Size: 3% base plus 3% green shoe, fully exercised — over 5.80 crore shares, about 6% of equity.
Floor price: Rs 514 — reported as roughly 10% below the prevailing market price.
Against the year’s high: 32% below the 52-week high of Rs 759.20.
Retail discount: none offered to retail investors or employees.
Institutional subscription: 3.41 times.
Retail: 5.65 times.
Government holding: 66.14% → approximately 60.14%.
Proceeds: about Rs 3,000 crore, on shares offered at the floor price.
Gross in-situ metal value represented by the stake: about Rs 53,000 crore at the September 7 record price.
Copper record: US$14,533 a tonne, September 7 — twelve days after the sale closed.
The Bids Say the Price was too Low
The clearest evidence that Rs 514 undervalued the asset came from the buyers themselves.
Institutional investors bid for more than 8.91 crore shares against 2.61 crore reserved for them, an oversubscription of 3.41 times on the opening day.
At an indicative price of Rs 520.35, those bids were worth over Rs 4,600 crore — chasing roughly Rs 1,340 crore of stock.

Demand was strong enough that the government exercised the entire green shoe option, doubling the sale from 3 per cent to 6 per cent. The retail tranche was oversubscribed 5.65 times the following day.
Hindustan Copper shares fell more than 6 percent on August 25 as the discounted offer opened.

An offer bid three and a half times over by institutions, and five and a half times over by retail investors, is not conventionally described as tightly priced. The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management said the issue drew an enthusiastic response and was oversubscribed on both days.
Who Bought has not Been Disclosed
The identities of the institutions that acquired the stake have not been made public.
Offers for sale do not require buyer-level disclosure, and no bulk-deal filings naming the purchasers of the bulk of the stake have been published.
At least 25 per cent of the offer was reserved for mutual funds and insurance companies. Beyond that, the composition of the buying is unknown to the public that owned the asset.
What is on record is the starting position.

As of June 30, 2026, foreign portfolio investors held 5.96 per cent of Hindustan Copper and Life Insurance Corporation held 2.83 per cent. Whether foreign funds increased their holding through the August sale, and by how much, will not be visible until the September quarter shareholding pattern is filed.
For a company that holds one hundred per cent of India’s operating copper mining leases, that is an accountability gap of some consequence.
Rs 3,000 crore, in Context

The Centre has set a disinvestment and asset-monetisation target of Rs 80,000 crore for 2026-27, and had raised Rs 52,716 crore across eight public sector undertakings and SUUTI remittances by the time of the Hindustan Copper sale.
The proceeds from Hindustan Copper represent under 4 percent of that annual target.
Officials have signalled that further public sector stake sales will follow.
Questions that Require Answers
On what valuation basis was Rs 514 fixed, and was the in-situ value of the underlying resource considered at all in setting it?
2. Why was the sale timed to August 2026, with copper in a documented structural deficit and the LME approaching record highs?
3. Why was the green shoe exercised in full — doubling the sale — once it was evident the offer was oversubscribed 3.41 times, rather than repricing it?
Who acquired the stake? What proportion went to foreign portfolio investors, and will the government disclose the buyer composition?
5. Was any inter-ministerial assessment sought from the Ministry of Mines or the National Security Council Secretariat on diluting a sole-source strategic mineral asset?

6. Given that the United States has classified copper as critical and China has imposed security screening on foreign investment in its mines, what is India’s stated policy on foreign ownership of its only copper miner?
Is any further dilution of the remaining 60.14 per cent contemplated, and at what floor?
The Other Side

The government’s defence is available and should be stated. Offers for sale are routinely priced at a discount to clear volume; a floor is not a ceiling, and final allotment can occur above it. Strong oversubscription may be read as validating the process rather than condemning it.

The Centre retains a commanding 60.14 per cent and full operational control. The shares were sold into a listed market open to domestic and foreign investors alike. Nothing about the transaction was irregular, and no rule appears to have been broken.
Nor is the copper thesis unanimous. LME inventories rose from about 140,000 tonnes to over 330,000 tonnes within months, which some analysts argue is inconsistent with an acute deficit.
Goldman Sachs expects prices to moderate from records.

Resources are not reserves: only 156.97 million tonnes of the 767.37 million tonnes is classified as a proved-and-probable reserve, at a higher grade of 1.31 per cent, and the remainder may never be economically converted. The stock trades above 50 times trailing earnings. Execution has slipped before — output of 27,421 tonnes of metal-in-concentrate in 2025-26 missed guidance of about 30,000 tonnes, and the capacity target has already moved from the late 2020s to around 2030-31.

None of which answers the central question: whether a sovereign monopoly over a metal now classified as critical by the world’s largest economy, and stockpiled by its largest manufacturer, should have been sold down at a discount to fund a routine fiscal target — twelve days before that metal reached the highest price in recorded history.
The Question is not the 6 percent.
It is the Next Tranche.
The August sale is done. The more important question is what comes after it.

The government still owns about 60.14 per cent. If the logic of disinvestment is applied mechanically, another tranche will eventually be tempting. Copper is high. The stock is high. The fiscal target is always there.
But selling the next 5 percent would not be the same transaction repeated.
It would be another piece of a strategic monopoly leaving government hands — in a decade when every other major economy is moving to secure exactly this kind of asset rather than monetise it.

The Centre should therefore answer a larger question than why it sold 6 percent. Does India intend to retain controlling ownership of its only domestic copper miner for strategic reasons — or is Hindustan Copper simply another line item in the annual disinvestment spreadsheet?
The government can find Rs 3,000 crore elsewhere.
It cannot find another Hindustan Copper.
A Note on Method

This report alleges no illegality, no impropriety and no concealment by any individual, official or institution, and makes no claim of undisclosed reserves. Story is an analysis of policy decision and writers own opinion based on factual data. Hindustan Copper reports its mineral inventory in accordance with standard classification.

Every transactional figure — offer size, floor price, discount, subscription levels, stake reduction and disinvestment totals — is drawn from exchange filings and published reports cited below. The Rs 8.9 lakh crore and Rs 53,000 crore figures are gross in-situ metal values, computed arithmetically from the company’s own reported tonnage and grade at the September 7 LME price.

They are illustrations of scale, not valuations of the company or of the shares sold: in-situ metal is never fully recoverable, and no mining company trades at that value. The approximate realisation of Rs 3,000 crore is computed from shares offered at the floor price, not a reported settlement figure. The buyers of the stake are not publicly identified and this report does not speculate as to their identity.
The questions posed above are put for answer, not asserted as findings.
Not investment advice. Figures are current to mid-September 2026.
